script.opening: "I stuck myself with a used needle at work about an hour ago — it bled a bit. I’m really panicking — what if the patient had HIV or hepatitis? Have I caught something? What do I need to do right now?"

facts.text: Healthcare assistant on a medical ward. About an hour ago, while clearing a tray, a used hollow needle that had been used to take blood ("there was blood in it") went through her glove into her left index finger. It bled a little.
"I rinsed it under the tap." Didn’t squeeze it or wash with soap. Hasn’t reported it yet; came off the ward to ring the surgery because "I didn’t know who to tell".

"It was a used needle from a patient. I don’t know much more than that." The tray came from a bay of four patients; the nurse in charge would know which one. Doesn’t know their HIV or hepatitis status.

"I’d have to check my records" — had hepatitis B jabs when she started 3 years ago, not sure if she had a blood test afterwards. Well, no medicines, on the combined pill. Not pregnant (last period 2 weeks ago). Not breastfeeding. No allergies.
Hospital has an occupational health department (open 8–4 weekdays; it is 11am Tuesday). Mid-shift; worried about leaving the ward short-staffed.
Lives with her partner, Tom. They don’t use condoms.

Panicky, talking fast, close to tears. Calm down if the doctor gives clear, step-by-step instructions. Ask: "Today? I’m on shift," "And hepatitis?" and "What are the actual chances?" Agree to go straight to occupational health.

ice.ideas: "I’ve got HIV. It’s already too late."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of passing something to Tom, and of getting in trouble for not disposing of the needle properly.
ice.expectations: "Tell me exactly what to do, right now."

cues: "I rinsed it" — first aid to complete and check.
"I’m on shift" — the time-critical need to go now despite work pressure.
"We don’t use condoms" (if asked about partners) — advice on precautions until follow-up tests.

checkpoints.text: Gives immediate FIRST AID — encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water (no scrubbing/sucking), irrigate mucosa/eyes
Performs a structured RISK ASSESSMENT (percutaneous vs mucosal, hollow vs solid needle, depth, visible blood, source-patient HIV/HBV/HCV status/risk)
Refers URGENTLY to OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH/A&E for assessment and bloods (recipient baseline + source testing with consent sought by someone else) and reports the incident — the same day, without delay

Considers HIV PEP as TIME-CRITICAL (ASAP, ideally within 24 hours, not beyond 72 hours; not indicated if the source is undetectable on treatment for 6 months or more) based on risk, asking about pregnancy and medicines, via occ-health/specialist guidance (BHIVA/BASHH 2021)

Manages HEPATITIS B (vaccination status/booster, immunoglobulin if non-immune + high-risk source) and HEPATITIS C (no PEP; baseline + follow-up testing for seroconversion — HCV RNA at 6 and 12 weeks, anti-HCV at 12 and 24 weeks)
Provides REASSURANCE and psychological support, acknowledges the anxiety, explains that single-exposure transmission risk is generally low, and checks understanding
Calmly contains her panic and gives a clear step-by-step of what happens next and the timeline (first aid, bloods, occupational health, possible PEP), confirming she knows where to go now

Safety-nets and follows up: incident reporting, condoms and no blood donation until follow-up is complete, baseline and follow-up testing per protocol, urgent occ-health/PEP pathway, and review — structured, time-critical management, not delay

worked.txt: "Let’s act now. Make the wound bleed gently and wash it under running water with soap — don’t scrub or suck it. You’ve done the right thing coming straight away; time matters here."
"A few quick questions: was it a deep jab with a hollow needle, was there visible blood, and do we know anything about the patient — any HIV or hepatitis risk? That tells us how urgently we act."

"I’m sending you straight to occupational health (or the emergency department) for proper assessment and baseline blood tests, and they’ll arrange for the source patient to be asked for consent to be tested — that’s done by someone else, not you. Please also report it through your workplace incident system today."

"If there’s a real HIV risk, there’s preventive medication — PEP — that works best started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, and it isn’t given after three days. Is there any chance you could be pregnant, and do you take any medicines? That’s why this is time-critical."

"We’ll check your hepatitis B vaccination is up to date and boost it if needed, and possibly give protective antibody if the source is high-risk. Hepatitis C has no jab, so we test now and again over the next weeks to catch it early if it happened."

"I know this is frightening, but the chance of catching something from a single jab is generally low — for HIV, even from a known positive untreated source, about 3 in 1,000 — and the whole system is set up to protect you. Until your follow-up tests are done, use condoms and don’t give blood. We’ll arrange your follow-up tests and support you throughout."

f.learning: A NEEDLESTICK/sharps exposure needs a structured, time-critical response. Start with immediate FIRST AID: encourage the wound to bleed, wash with soap and running water (do not scrub or suck), and irrigate mucosa/eyes for splashes. RISK-ASSESS the exposure — percutaneous versus mucosal/non-intact skin, hollow-bore (higher risk) versus solid needle, depth, visible blood, and the SOURCE patient’s HIV/HBV/HCV status/risk. Refer urgently, the same day, to OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH (or the emergency department) for assessment and bloods — recipient baseline serology and source testing with the source’s consent, sought by someone other than the exposed worker — and report the incident (Sharps Regulations 2013; RIDDOR if the source is known to carry a blood-borne virus). Consider HIV POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP), started as soon as possible (ideally within 24 hours, not beyond 72 hours; 28 days; not indicated if the source is undetectable on treatment for at least 6 months with good adherence; check pregnancy and interactions — BHIVA/BASHH 2021), so assessment is time-critical and made via occ-health/specialist guidance. For HEPATITIS B, check/ensure vaccination status (booster/accelerated course if needed) and give HBV immunoglobulin if the recipient is non-immune with a high-risk/positive source; for HEPATITIS C there is no vaccine or PEP, so perform baseline and follow-up testing (HCV RNA at 6 and 12 weeks, anti-HCV at 12 and 24 weeks) to detect seroconversion with early antiviral treatment if it occurs. Advise condoms and no blood or tissue donation until follow-up is complete. Ensure incident reporting, baseline and follow-up testing per protocol, and provide reassurance and psychological support — acknowledging the significant anxiety while explaining that single-exposure transmission risk is generally low — and safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: [1] UK Guideline for the use of HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis 2021 (BHIVA/BASHH) · [2] Green Book chapter 18: Hepatitis B (UKHSA, updated February 2026) · [3] Guidance on the investigation and management of occupational exposure to hepatitis C (PHLS Advisory Committee on Blood Borne Viruses, now UKHSA) · [4] Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 and RIDDOR 2013 (HSE) · [5] GMC: Confidentiality (consent for source testing)
knowledge.summary: First aid now, then same-day (ideally immediate) assessment by occupational health or the emergency department. HIV PEP works best started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, and is not offered after 72 hours [1]. Hepatitis B protection depends on her vaccine response and the source [2]; hepatitis C has no PEP, so follow-up testing detects infection early for treatment [3].

points.t: Encourage the wound to bleed gently, wash with soap and running water, do not scrub or suck, cover with a waterproof dressing. Mucosal or eye splashes: irrigate with plenty of water [1][2].

Percutaneous injuries carry more risk than splashes; a hollow needle, deep injury, visible blood or a device that was in a vein or artery increase risk. The source’s status matters most: known HIV, HBV or HCV, or risk factors. The average HIV risk from a needlestick with HIV-positive blood is about 0.3% (1 in 333) [1].

Start as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, and not beyond 72 hours; a 28-day course. First-line is tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine with raltegravir [1]. If the source has been on treatment for at least 6 months with an undetectable viral load and good adherence, PEP is not indicated [1]. Check pregnancy and interacting medicines.

Known responders: a booster after a significant exposure to a known or high-risk source. Unvaccinated or incomplete course: an accelerated vaccine course, with hepatitis B immunoglobulin if the source is known or high-risk. Known non-responders: immunoglobulin [2]. Occupational health checks her anti-HBs.
No vaccine or PEP. Baseline blood stored; after a known or likely infected source, HCV RNA at 6 and 12 weeks and anti-HCV at 12 and 24 weeks, so infection is treated early [3].
The source is tested for HIV, HBV and HCV only with their consent, sought by someone other than the exposed worker [1][5].

Report the incident to the employer. Employers must record and investigate sharps injuries and provide access to treatment [4]; an injury from a source known to carry a blood-borne virus is reportable under RIDDOR [4].
Use condoms and avoid blood or tissue donation until follow-up is complete; occupational health advises on any work implications [1].

ro.d: Picked up “is it already too late?” and answered it with the time window.
Idea (she has HIV), concern (too late), expectation (clear instructions).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of passing something to Tom, and of getting in trouble for not disposing of the needle properly — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Erin, I’m Dr Ahmed. Tell me what happened.
model.why: Open start, brief because time matters

model.text: I stuck myself with a used needle at work about an hour ago. It bled a bit. I’m really panicking. What if the patient had HIV or hepatitis? Have I caught something? What do I need to do right now?
You’ve done exactly the right thing coming straight in. We’ll go step by step, and quickly. Have you washed it yet?
I rinsed it.
Let’s make sure. Let it bleed gently, wash under running soapy water now at the sink here, don’t scrub or suck it, then I’ll put a dressing on.
Now, what kind of needle was it, and how deep? Was there visible blood on it? Had it been in a vein?
It was a used needle from a patient. I don’t know much more than that.
Do you know anything about the patient: whether they have HIV, hepatitis B or C, or any risk factors? It’s fine if you don’t.
I don’t know.
Have you had the hepatitis B vaccine, and do you know if you responded to it?
I’d have to check my records.
Occupational health will check that. Is there any chance you could be pregnant, and do you take any medicines?
I don’t think so. I’d need to check.
What’s going through your mind right now?
That I’ve got HIV. That it’s already too late.
It isn’t too late. The timing is on your side, and that’s why we act today. What are you hoping I can do?
Tell me what to do.

Here’s the plan. You need to be seen by occupational health straight away, or the emergency department if they’re not available now. They’ll take a baseline blood sample, check your hepatitis B protection, and arrange for the patient to be asked for consent to be tested. That’s done by someone else, not you.
model.why: Urgent referral; baseline bloods; source testing with consent

model.text: Today? I’m on shift.

Today, now. This comes first, and your manager needs to know anyway. There’s a medicine called PEP that lowers the chance of HIV. It works best started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, and it isn’t given after three days. The team decides whether you need it from the risk.
And hepatitis?

For hepatitis B, depending on your vaccine response and the patient’s status, you may get a booster, a faster vaccine course, or an antibody injection. Hepatitis C has no jab or PEP, so they’ll repeat blood tests over the next few months. If it did happen, catching it early means it can be treated and cured.
model.why: HBV (Green Book ch 18) and HCV follow-up

model.text: What are the actual chances?
For HIV, even when the patient definitely has it and isn’t treated, the risk from one needlestick is about 3 in 1,000. Most sources are negative. That’s low, and PEP lowers it further.
Okay. That helps.
Please report it through your workplace incident system today too. Until your follow-up tests are done, use condoms, don’t give blood, and occupational health will talk to you about work.

If you start PEP and get side effects, a rash, or feel unwell, contact the team who prescribed it. If you develop a fever, rash or flu-like illness in the coming weeks, tell them too. How are you getting there now?
model.why: Safety-net for PEP and seroconversion illness

model.text: I’ll go straight from here.
Tell me the plan in your own words.
Occupational health or A&E now, bloods, maybe PEP, hepatitis B check, report it, condoms until the tests are done.
That’s it. And this is frightening, so if the worry gets too much while you wait for results, come back and talk to us. I’m going to write down the time of the injury for you to take with you.

social.t: Waiting for results is stressful; offer support and check in.
Condoms until follow-up is complete; offer to help her explain this to a partner if she wishes.

legal.t: Employers must record and investigate sharps injuries and ensure access to medical advice and PEP (Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013).
A sharps injury from a source known to carry a blood-borne virus is reportable to the HSE by the employer (RIDDOR 2013).
The source patient can only be tested with consent (GMC confidentiality).

professional.t: Occupational health leads PEP, vaccination and follow-up testing, and advises on any work implications.
Record the time of injury, first aid, advice and referral.

community.t: The emergency department provides PEP assessment when occupational health is closed; sexual health clinics can also advise.

pitfalls.intro: This is a time-critical station. Candidates fail by managing it slowly in the practice, by missing the PEP window, and by forgetting hepatitis B, hepatitis C follow-up and reporting.

items.why: Bleeding and washing are the first step whatever the source.
items.fix: Check on the phone that it has been done properly.

items.fail: Routine bloods and a review next week.
items.why: PEP works best within hours and is not given after 72 hours (BHIVA 2021).
Protection depends on vaccine response and source (Green Book ch 18).
items.fix: Ask about vaccination; occupational health checks anti-HBs.

items.fail: Telling her to ask the source patient.
items.why: Consent must be sought by someone else.
items.fix: Occupational health arranges source consent and testing.

items.fail: Dismissing the panic, or feeding it.
items.why: Honest numbers reduce fear and support adherence.
items.fix: About 3 in 1,000 for HIV from a known positive source, lower with PEP.

items.why: Employers must record sharps injuries; precautions protect partners until follow-up.
items.fix: Incident report, condoms, no blood donation until follow-up complete.

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened it’s too late. It isn’t: you’ve come within the hour, and that’s exactly when this works best.”
management.psychosocial: Free her from the shift; offer support while awaiting results.
sharedPlan: First aid now; occupational health or ED immediately
Baseline bloods; source testing with consent; PEP decision (BHIVA 2021); HBV by vaccine response (Green Book ch 18)
HCV follow-up testing; incident report; condoms and no blood donation until follow-up complete
safetyNet: PEP side effects or rash: contact the prescribing team
Fever, rash or flu-like illness in the following weeks: tell occupational health
Anxiety becoming overwhelming: return to the practice

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a time-critical station. Candidates fail by managing it slowly in the practice, by missing the PEP window, and by forgetting hepatitis B, hepatitis C follow-up and reporting.

items.why: Bleeding and washing are the first step whatever the source.
items.fix: Check on the phone that it has been done properly.

items.fail: Routine bloods and a review next week.
items.why: PEP works best within hours and is not given after 72 hours (BHIVA 2021).
Protection depends on vaccine response and source (Green Book ch 18).
items.fix: Ask about vaccination; occupational health checks anti-HBs.

items.fail: Telling her to ask the source patient.
items.why: Consent must be sought by someone else.
items.fix: Occupational health arranges source consent and testing.

items.fail: Dismissing the panic, or feeding it.
items.why: Honest numbers reduce fear and support adherence.
items.fix: About 3 in 1,000 for HIV from a known positive source, lower with PEP.

items.why: Employers must record sharps injuries; precautions protect partners until follow-up.
items.fix: Incident report, condoms, no blood donation until follow-up complete.
